changes.after: A pattern can check the shape of a hash. A guard adds a test after the shape matches.

before: case/in patterns inspect structure. This hash pattern requires kind: :note and an Integer count. Integer => n both checks that value and binds it to n. Extra hash keys are allowed by this pattern.

The if n > 0 guard is checked after the pattern matches. A false guard means this branch is not selected; the explicit else handles unmatched cases. This is different from treating every non-nil count as acceptable.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
entry = {kind: :note, count: 2}
case entry
in {kind: :note, count: Integer => n} if n > 0
  puts n
else
  puts "skip"
end
```
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
